claim: The ventral pallidum (VP) is a critical node in the neural circuitry underlying reward-related behaviors.
source: The ventral pallidum (VP) is a critical node in the neural circuitry underlying reward-related behaviors (Creed et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2009), including relapse to drug and alcohol seeking (Farrell et al., 2018; Kalivas and Volkow, 2005; Saunders et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing VP's role in reward circuitry.

claim: VP is critical for relapse to drug and alcohol seeking.
source: The ventral pallidum (VP) is a critical node in the neural circuitry underlying reward-related behaviors (Creed et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2009), including relapse to drug and alcohol seeking (Farrell et al., 2018; Kalivas and Volkow, 2005; Saunders et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on drug and alcohol relapse.

claim: Neurons in the VP respond to primary rewards.
source: Neurons in the VP are known to respond to a variety of reward-related stimuli, including primary rewards (Itoga et al., 2016; Tindell et al., 2006), Pavlovian cues predicting reward delivery (Smith et al., 2011; Tindell et al., 2005; 2009), cues predicting reward availability (Richard et al., 2016), and cues indicating specific appropriate reward-seeking actions (Ito and Doya, 2009; Tachibana and Hikosaka, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: VP neurons respond to Pavlovian cues predicting reward delivery.
source: Neurons in the VP are known to respond to a variety of reward-related stimuli, including primary rewards (Itoga et al., 2016; Tindell et al., 2006), Pavlovian cues predicting reward delivery (Smith et al., 2011; Tindell et al., 2005; 2009), cues predicting reward availability (Richard et al., 2016), and cues indicating specific appropriate reward-seeking actions (Ito and Doya, 2009; Tachibana and Hikosaka, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies on VP responses to Pavlovian cues.

claim: VP neurons respond to cues predicting reward availability.
source: Neurons in the VP are known to respond to a variety of reward-related stimuli, including primary rewards (Itoga et al., 2016; Tindell et al., 2006), Pavlovian cues predicting reward delivery (Smith et al., 2011; Tindell et al., 2005; 2009), cues predicting reward availability (Richard et al., 2016), and cues indicating specific appropriate reward-seeking actions (Ito and Doya, 2009; Tachibana and Hikosaka, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: VP neurons respond to cues indicating specific appropriate reward-seeking actions.
source: Neurons in the VP are known to respond to a variety of reward-related stimuli, including primary rewards (Itoga et al., 2016; Tindell et al., 2006), Pavlovian cues predicting reward delivery (Smith et al., 2011; Tindell et al., 2005; 2009), cues predicting reward availability (Richard et al., 2016), and cues indicating specific appropriate reward-seeking actions (Ito and Doya, 2009; Tachibana and Hikosaka, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Activity in VP is critical for normal levels of cue-elicited reward seeking across a variety of paradigms.
source: Further, activity in VP is critical for normal levels of cue-elicited reward seeking across a variety of paradigms (Leung and Balleine, 2015; Mahler et al., 2014; Prasad and McNally, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies demonstrating VP's role in reward seeking.

claim: The VP has been historically suggested to act as a motor expression site for a 'limbic-motor' interface.
source: While historically the VP has been suggested to act as a motor expression site for a 'limbic-motor' interface (Heimer et al., 1982; Mogenson et al., 1980) due to its close connections with motor output regions, more recent work has suggested a greater role for VP in reward processing itself.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to historical literature on VP function.

claim: Recent work has suggested a greater role for VP in reward processing itself.
source: While historically the VP has been suggested to act as a motor expression site for a 'limbic-motor' interface (Heimer et al., 1982; Mogenson et al., 1980) due to its close connections with motor output regions, more recent work has suggested a greater role for VP in reward processing itself.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from recent literature contrasting with historical views.

claim: VP responses to cues have been argued to contribute to reward seeking by representing expected reward value.
source: For instance, VP responses to cues have been argued to contribute to reward seeking by representing expected reward value (Tachibana and Hikosaka, 2012), but have also been suggested to encode state and action values (Ito and Doya, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior study proposing this interpretation.

claim: VP responses to cues have been suggested to encode state and action values.
source: For instance, VP responses to cues have been argued to contribute to reward seeking by representing expected reward value (Tachibana and Hikosaka, 2012), but have also been suggested to encode state and action values (Ito and Doya, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior study proposing this interpretation.

claim: VP neurons encode the incentive value of cues, as defined by their ability to invigorate instrumental reward-seeking actions.
source: Previously, we showed that VP neurons encode the incentive value of cues, as defined by their ability to invigorate instrumental reward-seeking actions (Richard et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Rats trained in the DS task and Pavlovian conditioning did not differ in the number of training days required to meet training criteria.
source: Rats trained in the two tasks did not differ in the number of training days required to meet training criteria (Figure 1E; t(10)=0.1249, p=0.9031, Bayes factor of 2.112 in favor of the null).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1E showing training days.

claim: Most recording sites were centered in middle to slightly caudal locations in VP (0 to 0.24 mm behind bregma).
source: Most recording sites were centered in middle to slightly caudal locations in VP (0 to 0.24 mm behind bregma), though one rat trained in the Pavlovian task had electrodes centered more caudally (~0.5 mm caudal to bregma).
evidence: The claim is based on histological verification of recording locations.

claim: The DS elicited increases in activity in 60% of VP units (189/314).
source: The DS elicited increases in activity in 60% of VP units (189/314) and decreases in activity in 27% of units (85/314).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of neural responses.

claim: The DS elicited decreases in activity in 27% of VP units (85/314).
source: The DS elicited increases in activity in 60% of VP units (189/314) and decreases in activity in 27% of units (85/314).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of neural responses.

claim: 48.7% of VP neurons were excited by the CS+ (191/392).
source: A smaller, but still robust, population of VP neurons responded to the CS+, including 48.7% of VP neurons that were excited by the CS+ (191/392) and 20.9% of VP neurons that were inhibited (82/392).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of neural responses.

claim: 20.9% of VP neurons were inhibited by the CS+ (82/392).
source: A smaller, but still robust, population of VP neurons responded to the CS+, including 48.7% of VP neurons that were excited by the CS+ (191/392) and 20.9% of VP neurons that were inhibited (82/392).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of neural responses.

claim: The proportion of cue-responsive neurons differed across the instrumental and Pavlovian tasks.
source: While the proportion of cue-responsive neurons differed across the two tasks (x2 = 30.34, p<0.001), we next assessed whether these cue responses encoded learned value or behavioral responses similarly.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (chi-squared test) of proportions.

claim: Most DS excited neurons were significantly more excited by the DS than the NS (132/189, 69.8%).
source: Most DS excited neurons were significantly more excited by the DS than the NS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; 132/189, 69.8%), whereas only 23.5% of DS-inhibited neurons were more inhibited by the DS than the NS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; 20/85, 6% of the whole population; Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Only 23.5% of DS-inhibited neurons were more inhibited by the DS than the NS (20/85).
source: Most DS excited neurons were significantly more excited by the DS than the NS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; 132/189, 69.8%), whereas only 23.5% of DS-inhibited neurons were more inhibited by the DS than the NS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; 20/85, 6% of the whole population; Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: DS-excited neurons as a population responded significantly more to the DS than the NS.
source: As a population, DS-excited neurons responded significantly more to the DS and the NS (Figure 3E; t[197]=15.43, p<0.001) and DS-inhibited neurons were more inhibited by the DS than by the NS (Figure 3G; t[84]=–3.10, p=0.0027), suggesting that both response types encode cue value.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to Figure 3E.

claim: DS-inhibited neurons as a population were more inhibited by the DS than by the NS.
source: As a population, DS-excited neurons responded significantly more to the DS and the NS (Figure 3E; t[197]=15.43, p<0.001) and DS-inhibited neurons were more inhibited by the DS than by the NS (Figure 3G; t[84]=–3.10, p=0.0027), suggesting that both response types encode cue value.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to Figure 3G.

claim: Both DS excitations and inhibitions encode cue value.
source: As a population, DS-excited neurons responded significantly more to the DS and the NS (Figure 3E; t[197]=15.43, p<0.001) and DS-inhibited neurons were more inhibited by the DS than by the NS (Figure 3G; t[84]=–3.10, p=0.0027), suggesting that both response types encode cue value.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential responses to DS vs NS in both excited and inhibited populations.

claim: The majority of CS+ excited neurons (64%, 123/191) were more excited by the CS+ than by the CS–.
source: VP neurons also encoded learned cue value in the Pavlovian task: the majority of CS+ excited neurons were more excited by the CS+ than by the CS– (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; 64%; 123/191; 31.4% of the population), though only a small fraction of CS+ inhibited neurons were more inhibited by the CS+ than by the CS– (8.3%; 7/84;~2% of the whole population; Figure 3D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Only a small fraction of CS+ inhibited neurons (8.3%, 7/84) were more inhibited by the CS+ than by the CS–.
source: VP neurons also encoded learned cue value in the Pavlovian task: the majority of CS+ excited neurons were more excited by the CS+ than by the CS– (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; 64%; 123/191; 31.4% of the population), though only a small fraction of CS+ inhibited neurons were more inhibited by the CS+ than by the CS– (8.3%; 7/84;~2% of the whole population; Figure 3D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: CS+ excited neurons as a population were significantly more excited by the CS+ than by the CS–.
source: As a population, CS+ excited neurons were significantly more excited by the CS+ than by the CS– (Figure 3G; t[190]=18.6890, p<0.001) and CS+ inhibited neurons were also more inhibited by the CS+ than by the CS– (Figure 2H; t[83]=-−2.72, p=0.01), indicating that, like VP responses in the instrumental task, both excitations and inhibitions predict cue value after Pavlovian conditioning.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to Figure 3G.

claim: CS+ inhibited neurons as a population were more inhibited by the CS+ than by the CS–.
source: As a population, CS+ excited neurons were significantly more excited by the CS+ than by the CS– (Figure 3G; t[190]=18.6890, p<0.001) and CS+ inhibited neurons were also more inhibited by the CS+ than by the CS– (Figure 2H; t[83]=-−2.72, p=0.01), indicating that, like VP responses in the instrumental task, both excitations and inhibitions predict cue value after Pavlovian conditioning.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to Figure 2H.

claim: Both excitations and inhibitions predict cue value after Pavlovian conditioning.
source: As a population, CS+ excited neurons were significantly more excited by the CS+ than by the CS– (Figure 3G; t[190]=18.6890, p<0.001) and CS+ inhibited neurons were also more inhibited by the CS+ than by the CS– (Figure 2H; t[83]=-−2.72, p=0.01), indicating that, like VP responses in the instrumental task, both excitations and inhibitions predict cue value after Pavlovian conditioning.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential responses to CS+ vs CS– in both excited and inhibited populations.

claim: There was no difference in the population auROC distributions for the DS versus the CS+ for predicting cue identity.
source: We found no difference in the population auROC distributions for the DS versus the CS+ for predicting cue identity (Figure 3I; t[704]=1.22, p=0.22; Bayes factor of 5.706 favoring the null), suggesting that VP firing encodes cue value equally in both tasks.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test and Bayes factor) and reference to Figure 3I.

claim: VP firing encodes cue value equally in both instrumental and Pavlovian tasks.
source: We found no difference in the population auROC distributions for the DS versus the CS+ for predicting cue identity (Figure 3I; t[704]=1.22, p=0.22; Bayes factor of 5.706 favoring the null), suggesting that VP firing encodes cue value equally in both tasks.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of difference in auROC distributions between tasks.

claim: Post-cue firing was significantly more predictive of cue identity than pre-cue firing for both the instrumental and Pavlovian tasks.
source: Post-cue firing was significantly more predictive of cue identity than pre-cue firing for both the instrumental (t[313]=11.8213, p<0.001) and the Pavlovian task (t[391]=11.0872, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparisons (t-tests) of pre- and post-cue firing predictiveness.

claim: DS excited neurons were more likely to be inhibited by the control cue (NS) than CS+ excited neurons were to be inhibited by the CS–.
source: While cue responses were equally predictive of cue identity for the instrumental and Pavlovian tasks, DS excited neurons were more likely to be inhibited by the control cue (the NS) than CS+ excited neurons were to be inhibited by the CS– (Figure 3J; x2 = 63.9923, p<0.001), perhaps suggesting a more active role for response inhibition by the neurons in the instrumental task.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (chi-squared test) and reference to Figure 3J.

claim: About 20% of DS-excited neurons (24/130) are significantly more responsive to the DS when it is followed by a response.
source: When assessed individually (Figure 4A), about 20% of DS-excited neurons are significantly more responsive to the DS when it is followed by a response (24/130) and 16% of DS-inhibited neurons are more responsive on trials with a response (14/85).
evidence: The claim is supported by individual neuron analysis and reference to Figure 4A.

claim: 16% of DS-inhibited neurons (14/85) are more responsive on trials with a response.
source: When assessed individually (Figure 4A), about 20% of DS-excited neurons are significantly more responsive to the DS when it is followed by a response (24/130) and 16% of DS-inhibited neurons are more responsive on trials with a response (14/85).
evidence: The claim is supported by individual neuron analysis.

claim: Only ~9% of CS+ excited neurons (14/160) were more excited on trials with a response.
source: Only ~9% of CS+ excited neurons (Figure 4B) were more excited on trials with a response (14/160) and ~5% of CS+ inhibited neurons are more responsive (3/66).
evidence: The claim is supported by individual neuron analysis and reference to Figure 4B.

claim: ~5% of CS+ inhibited neurons (3/66) are more responsive on trials with a response.
source: Only ~9% of CS+ excited neurons (Figure 4B) were more excited on trials with a response (14/160) and ~5% of CS+ inhibited neurons are more responsive (3/66).
evidence: The claim is supported by individual neuron analysis.

claim: DS-excited neurons as a population were significantly more excited on trials when the DS was followed by a response.
source: As a population, DS-excited neurons (130 units) were significantly more excited on trials when the DS was followed by a response (Figures 4E and 3I; t[129]=8.60, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to Figures 4E and 3I.

claim: DS-inhibited neurons as a population were more inhibited on trials with a response.
source: DS-inhibited neurons (67 units) were also more inhibited on trials with a response (Figure 3F and I; t[66]=–4.66, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to Figures 3F and I.

claim: CS+ excited neurons as a population were more excited on trials with a response.
source: Similarly, CS+ excited neurons (174 units) were more excited on trials with a response (Figure 4G and J; t[174]=10.08, p<0.001), though CS+ inhibited neurons (82 units) did not distinguish between trials with and without a response (Figure 4H and J; t[81]=.479, p=0.633; Bayes factor: null is 6.46 times more likely than the alternative).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to Figures 4G and J.

claim: CS+ inhibited neurons as a population did not distinguish between trials with and without a response.
source: Similarly, CS+ excited neurons (174 units) were more excited on trials with a response (Figure 4G and J; t[174]=10.08, p<0.001), though CS+ inhibited neurons (82 units) did not distinguish between trials with and without a response (Figure 4H and J; t[81]=.479, p=0.633; Bayes factor: null is 6.46 times more likely than the alternative).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test and Bayes factor) and reference to Figures 4H and J.

claim: Post-DS firing was significantly more predictive of port entry likelihood than post-CS+ firing.
source: Post-DS firing was significantly more predictive of port entry likelihood than post-CS+ firing (Figure 4C and D; t[704]=3.49, p<0.001), though post-cue firing was predictive of port entry likelihood for both the instrumental task (t[313]=3.708, p<0.001), and the Pavlovian task (t[391]=2.697, p=0.0073).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (t-test) and reference to Figures 4C and D.

claim: Post-cue firing was predictive of port entry likelihood for both the instrumental and Pavlovian tasks.
source: Post-DS firing was significantly more predictive of port entry likelihood than post-CS+ firing (Figure 4C and D; t[704]=3.49, p<0.001), though post-cue firing was predictive of port entry likelihood for both the instrumental task (t[313]=3.708, p<0.001), and the Pavlovian task (t[391]=2.697, p=0.0073).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-tests) for both tasks.

claim: The post-DS firing rate of 62 units (19.75%) significantly predicted the animal's latency to make a port entry.
source: The post-DS firing rate of 62 units (19.75%) significantly predicted the animal's latency to make a port entry (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis and reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Only 14 units (3.57%) had post-CS+ firing rates that significantly predicted port entry latency.
source: By contrast, only 14 units (3.57%) had post-CS+ firing rates that significantly predicted port entry latency (Figure 5C), a much lower proportion of the population (DS versus CS+ % correlated: x2 = 47.477, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis and reference to Figure 5C.

claim: The proportion of latency-predicting neurons is significantly lower in the Pavlovian task than in the instrumental task.
source: By contrast, only 14 units (3.57%) had post-CS+ firing rates that significantly predicted port entry latency (Figure 5C), a much lower proportion of the population (DS versus CS+ % correlated: x2 = 47.477, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (chi-squared test) of proportions.

claim: The proportion of units with true post-DS firing that predicted the real latency was well outside the distribution of significantly correlated units from the shuffled datasets.
source: The proportion of units with true post-DS firing that predicted the real latency was well outside the distribution of significantly correlated units from the shuffled datasets (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), whereas the proportion of units in the Pavlovian task was not (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with shuffled control data and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: The proportion of units in the Pavlovian task that predicted latency was not outside the distribution from shuffled datasets.
source: The proportion of units with true post-DS firing that predicted the real latency was well outside the distribution of significantly correlated units from the shuffled datasets (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), whereas the proportion of units in the Pavlovian task was not (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with shuffled control data and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Only 9 units (2.8%) predicted latency in the Pavlovian task when assessed against shuffled latencies.
source: In addition, when we assessed the number of units with post-cue firing rates that were more predictive of the real latency than of the shuffled latencies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D), we found only 9 units (2.8%) that predicted latency in the Pavlovian task, versus 61 in the instrumental task (19.42%).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with shuffled control data and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: 61 units (19.42%) predicted latency in the instrumental task when assessed against shuffled latencies.
source: In addition, when we assessed the number of units with post-cue firing rates that were more predictive of the real latency than of the shuffled latencies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D), we found only 9 units (2.8%) that predicted latency in the Pavlovian task, versus 61 in the instrumental task (19.42%).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with shuffled control data and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Latency-predicting neurons are, on average, significantly excited by presentations of the DS.
source: Furthermore, while latency-predicting neurons are, on average, significantly excited by presentations of the DS (Figure 5D and G; t[61]=7.08, p<0.001; 48/62 units excited, 77.4%), latency-predicting neurons in the CS+ task are not (Figure 5E and H; t[13]=2.00, p=0.06650; 7/14 units excited; Bayes factor of 1.27 in favor of the alternative).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to Figures 5D and G.

claim: Latency-predicting neurons in the CS+ task are not significantly excited by the CS+.
source: Furthermore, while latency-predicting neurons are, on average, significantly excited by presentations of the DS (Figure 5D and G; t[61]=7.08, p<0.001; 48/62 units excited, 77.4%), latency-predicting neurons in the CS+ task are not (Figure 5E and H; t[13]=2.00, p=0.06650; 7/14 units excited; Bayes factor of 1.27 in favor of the alternative).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test and Bayes factor) and reference to Figures 5E and H.

claim: Latency-predicting neurons are more likely to be excited by the cue in the instrumental task than in the Pavlovian task.
source: Latency-predicting neurons are more likely to be excited by the cue in the instrumental task than in the Pavlovian task (x2 = 4.294, p=0.038246).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (chi-squared test) of proportions.

claim: The distribution of correlation coefficients was significantly more negative in the instrumental task than in the Pavlovian task.
source: For the population, the distribution of correlation coefficients was significantly more negative in the instrumental task than in the Pavlovian (Figure 5A and C; t[703]=2.0493, p=0.04), though the distribution is more negative in the 300 msec post-cue than in the 300 msec pre-cue in both the instrumental t[313]=–10.81, p<0.001) and Pavlovian tasks (t[390]=–﻿9.52, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (t-test) and reference to Figures 5A and C.

claim: The distribution of correlation coefficients is more negative in the 300 msec post-cue than in the 300 msec pre-cue in both the instrumental and Pavlovian tasks.
source: For the population, the distribution of correlation coefficients was significantly more negative in the instrumental task than in the Pavlovian (Figure 5A and C; t[703]=2.0493, p=0.04), though the distribution is more negative in the 300 msec post-cue than in the 300 msec pre-cue in both the instrumental t[313]=–10.81, p<0.001) and Pavlovian tasks (t[390]=–﻿9.52, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-tests) for both tasks.

claim: VP firing rates encode some information relating to the subsequent port entry latency in the Pavlovian task, though this encoding is much weaker than in the instrumental task.
source: This suggests that while latency encoding in the Pavlovian task is much weaker, VP firing rates do encode some information relating to the subsequent port entry latency.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the statistical findings showing weak but significant post-cue encoding in the Pavlovian task.

claim: The distribution of correlation coefficients in the Pavlovian task shifted negatively in the 50 msec window prior to cue onset.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the distribution of correlation coefficients in the Pavlovian task shifted negatively in the 50 msec window prior to cue onset (Figure 5F; q=3.532, p<0.05), suggesting that the weak relationship between post-CS+ firing and latency may be accounted for by trial-by-trial variation in firing rates, rather than in phasic cue responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5F.

claim: The weak relationship between post-CS+ firing and latency may be accounted for by trial-by-trial variation in firing rates, rather than in phasic cue responses.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the distribution of correlation coefficients in the Pavlovian task shifted negatively in the 50 msec window prior to cue onset (Figure 5F; q=3.532, p<0.05), suggesting that the weak relationship between post-CS+ firing and latency may be accounted for by trial-by-trial variation in firing rates, rather than in phasic cue responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the finding that correlation coefficients shifted before cue onset.

claim: The distribution of correlation coefficients in the DS task did not significantly differ from 0 until the window 50–100 msec post-DS.
source: By contrast, the distribution of correlation coefficients in the DS task did not significantly differ from 0 until the window 50–100 msec post-DS (Figure 5F; q=4.171, p<0.05), when phasic cue excitations are occurring in the bulk of correlated neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5F.

claim: Encoding of the latency of cue-elicited reward seeking by individual VP units and in the population is much stronger in the instrumental task than in the Pavlovian task.
source: Overall, encoding of the latency of cue-elicited reward seeking by individual VP units and in the population is much stronger in the instrumental task than in the Pavlovian task.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference from multiple statistical comparisons showing stronger latency encoding in the instrumental task.

claim: Variability in post-cue firing did not differ between the instrumental and Pavlovian tasks when comparing the whole population.
source: Variability in post-cue firing did not differ when comparing the whole population (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A; t[704]=–1.16, p=0.24; Bayes factor of 6.10 favoring the null) and was greater in the Pavlovian task when only the cue excited neurons were considered (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B; t[298]=2.75, p=0.0063).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test and Bayes factor) and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Variability in post-cue firing was greater in the Pavlovian task when only the cue excited neurons were considered.
source: Variability in post-cue firing did not differ when comparing the whole population (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A; t[704]=–1.16, p=0.24; Bayes factor of 6.10 favoring the null) and was greater in the Pavlovian task when only the cue excited neurons were considered (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B; t[298]=2.75, p=0.0063).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Post-cue port entry latency is more variable in the Pavlovian task.
source: In addition, post-cue port entry latency is more variable in the Pavlovian task (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D; z(95354)=−5.82, p<0.001), indicating that weak correlations between post-CS+ firing and latency are not due to low variability in post CS+ port entry latency.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Weak correlations between post-CS+ firing and latency are not due to low variability in post CS+ port entry latency.
source: In addition, post-cue port entry latency is more variable in the Pavlovian task (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D; z(95354)=−5.82, p<0.001), indicating that weak correlations between post-CS+ firing and latency are not due to low variability in post CS+ port entry latency.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the finding that latency variability is actually higher in the Pavlovian task.

claim: Instrumentally trained rats moved at greater velocities post-cue than Pavlovian trained rats.
source: Overall, although we found that velocity increased and distance from the port decreased shortly after cue onset for both tasks, instrumentally trained rats moved at greater velocities post-cue (F[1,118]=23.166, p<0.001) and were positioned at further distances from the port at cue onset (F[1,118]=6.99, p=0.009).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) of video tracking data.

claim: Instrumentally trained rats were positioned at further distances from the port at cue onset than Pavlovian trained rats.
source: Overall, although we found that velocity increased and distance from the port decreased shortly after cue onset for both tasks, instrumentally trained rats moved at greater velocities post-cue (F[1,118]=23.166, p<0.001) and were positioned at further distances from the port at cue onset (F[1,118]=6.99, p=0.009).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) of video tracking data.

claim: Rats trained under Pavlovian versus instrumental contingencies did not differ in the likelihood of movement onset during the first 300 ms post cue.
source: Rats trained under Pavlovian versus instrumental contingencies did not differ in the likelihood of movement onset during the first 300 ms post cue in which we assessed neural firing (13.3% of post-DS movement onsets and 8.3% of post-CS+ movement onsets; X2=0.345, p=0.56), and we did not observe a significant difference in movement-onset times (F[1,74]=1.365, p=0.24).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-squared test) of movement onset data.

claim: There was no significant difference in movement-onset times between rats trained under Pavlovian versus instrumental contingencies.
source: Rats trained under Pavlovian versus instrumental contingencies did not differ in the likelihood of movement onset during the first 300 ms post cue in which we assessed neural firing (13.3% of post-DS movement onsets and 8.3% of post-CS+ movement onsets; X2=0.345, p=0.56), and we did not observe a significant difference in movement-onset times (F[1,74]=1.365, p=0.24).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) of movement onset timing.

claim: Distance encoding significantly predicted latency encoding.
source: We found that the only significant single predictor of latency encoding was distance encoding, in that neurons that had greater post-cue firing rates on trials with shorter port entry latencies, also had greater post-cue firing on trials where the rat was closer to the port at cue onset (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A; F[1,140]=16.295, p<0.001), similar to results previously reported for the nucleus accumbens (McGinty et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: The relationship between encoding of proximity and vigor depended on training history.
source: This relationship between encoding of proximity and vigor depended on training history (F[1,140]=4.55, p=0.034), as distance encoding in the rats trained under a Pavlovian contingency was not significantly predictive of latency encoding (F[1,44]=2.09, p=0.15), whereas distance encoding robustly predicted latency encoding in instrumentally trained rats (F[1,96]=35.632, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-tests) showing an interaction with training history.

claim: Distance encoding in rats trained under a Pavlovian contingency was not significantly predictive of latency encoding.
source: This relationship between encoding of proximity and vigor depended on training history (F[1,140]=4.55, p=0.034), as distance encoding in the rats trained under a Pavlovian contingency was not significantly predictive of latency encoding (F[1,44]=2.09, p=0.15), whereas distance encoding robustly predicted latency encoding in instrumentally trained rats (F[1,96]=35.632, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) in the Pavlovian group.

claim: Distance encoding robustly predicted latency encoding in instrumentally trained rats.
source: This relationship between encoding of proximity and vigor depended on training history (F[1,140]=4.55, p=0.034), as distance encoding in the rats trained under a Pavlovian contingency was not significantly predictive of latency encoding (F[1,44]=2.09, p=0.15), whereas distance encoding robustly predicted latency encoding in instrumentally trained rats (F[1,96]=35.632, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) in the instrumental group.

claim: Latency encoding was not significantly predicted by the degree to which neurons encoded post-cue velocity.
source: Notably, latency encoding was not significantly predicted by the degree to which neurons encoded post-cue velocity (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B; F[1,140]=–0.335, p=0.56) or movement-onset latencies (Figure 5—figure supplement 5C; F[1,140]=1.83, p=0.17).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Latency encoding was not significantly predicted by the degree to which neurons encoded movement-onset latencies.
source: Notably, latency encoding was not significantly predicted by the degree to which neurons encoded post-cue velocity (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B; F[1,140]=–0.335, p=0.56) or movement-onset latencies (Figure 5—figure supplement 5C; F[1,140]=1.83, p=0.17).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: The relationship between distance and latency encoding was modulated by training history, suggesting a greater coupling between these variables and action in the instrumental task.
source: That the relationship between distance and latency encoding was modulated by training history suggests a greater coupling between these variables and action in the instrumental task.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the finding that distance-latency encoding relationship differs by training history.

claim: Rats made port entries at significantly shorter latencies during the reward cue than during the control cue by the end of training.
source: By the end of training, rats made port entries at significantly shorter latencies during the reward cue than during the control cue (main effect of cue: F[1,28]=25.314, p<0.001), regardless of training group (interaction of cue and training: F[1,28]=0.144, p=0.707; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Rats in both training groups increased their probability of port entry preferentially during the reward-related cue versus the control cue.
source: Rats in both training groups increased their probability of port entry preferentially during the reward-related cue versus the control cue (main effect of cue: F[1,28]=951.681, p<0.001), with rats trained under the instrumental contingency reaching a slightly higher response probability during the reward cue once they met training criteria (interaction of cue and training: F[1,28]=5.962, p=0.021; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Rats trained under the instrumental contingency reached a slightly higher response probability during the reward cue once they met training criteria.
source: Rats in both training groups increased their probability of port entry preferentially during the reward-related cue versus the control cue (main effect of cue: F[1,28]=951.681, p<0.001), with rats trained under the instrumental contingency reaching a slightly higher response probability during the reward cue once they met training criteria (interaction of cue and training: F[1,28]=5.962, p=0.021; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test showing interaction) and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Rats trained under Pavlovian conditioning required more days to reach training criteria (10.35 ± 0.23) than those trained under an instrumental contingency (9.07 ± 0.24).
source: On average, rats trained under the Pavlovian conditioning required more days to reach training criteria (10.35 ± 0.23) than those trained under an instrumental contingency (9.07 ± 0.24; t[29]=3.839, p<0.001; Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (t-test) and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: VP inactivation with baclofen and muscimol reduced the probability of port entry during the cue period in the instrumental task.
source: In the instrumental task, inactivation of VP with low doses of the GABA agonists baclofen and muscimol reduced the probability of port entry during the cue period (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B; main effect of treatment: F[4,130]=28.666, p<0.001; Sidak, p<0.001), and did so more strongly during the DS period than during the NS (interaction between treatment and cue identity: F[4,130]=7.205, p<0.001; DS Sidak, p<0.001; NS Sidak, n.s.).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test and post-hoc tests) and reference to figures.

claim: VP inactivation reduced port entry probability more strongly during the DS period than during the NS in the instrumental task.
source: In the instrumental task, inactivation of VP with low doses of the GABA agonists baclofen and muscimol reduced the probability of port entry during the cue period (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B; main effect of treatment: F[4,130]=28.666, p<0.001; Sidak, p<0.001), and did so more strongly during the DS period than during the NS (interaction between treatment and cue identity: F[4,130]=7.205, p<0.001; DS Sidak, p<0.001; NS Sidak, n.s.).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing an interaction and selective post-hoc effects.

claim: VP inactivation increased port entry latency during the DS in the instrumental task.
source: VP inactivation also increased port entry latency during the cue (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A; main effect of treatment: F[4,18.254]=4.574, p=0.01) also selectively during the DS (interaction between drug and cue: F[4,23.879]=4.354, p=0.009; DS Sidak, p=0.022; NS Sidak, n.s.).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test and post-hoc tests) and reference to figures.

claim: VP inactivation increased port entry latency selectively during the DS and not the NS in the instrumental task.
source: VP inactivation also increased port entry latency during the cue (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A; main effect of treatment: F[4,18.254]=4.574, p=0.01) also selectively during the DS (interaction between drug and cue: F[4,23.879]=4.354, p=0.009; DS Sidak, p=0.022; NS Sidak, n.s.).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing an interaction and selective post-hoc effects.

claim: VP inactivation during the Pavlovian task reduced the probability of port entry during the cue.
source: Inactivation of VP during the Pavlovian task similarly reduced the probability of port entry during the cue (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3B; main effect of treatment: F[4,112]=9.904, p<0.001; Sidak p<0.001), and did so selectively during the CS+ period (interaction between treatment and cue identity: F[4,112]=2.622, p=0.039; CS+ Sidak, p<0.001; CS- Sidak, n.s.).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test and post-hoc tests) and reference to figures.

claim: VP inactivation reduced port entry probability selectively during the CS+ period in the Pavlovian task.
source: Inactivation of VP during the Pavlovian task similarly reduced the probability of port entry during the cue (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3B; main effect of treatment: F[4,112]=9.904, p<0.001; Sidak p<0.001), and did so selectively during the CS+ period (interaction between treatment and cue identity: F[4,112]=2.622, p=0.039; CS+ Sidak, p<0.001; CS- Sidak, n.s.).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing an interaction and selective post-hoc effects.

claim: VP inactivation during the Pavlovian task had no significant effect on port entry latency.
source: In contrast to the instrumental task, VP inactivation during the Pavlovian task had no significant effect on port entry latency (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 3A; main effect of treatment: F[4,21.406]=1.059, p=0.401), regardless of cue identity (interaction between treatment and cue identity: F[4,18.061]=1.742, p=0.185).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) showing no significant effects and reference to figures.

claim: In both tasks, no drug treatment had any significant effect on port entry behavior during the inter-trial interval.
source: In both tasks, no drug treatment had any significant effect on port entry behavior during the inter-trial interval (main effect of treatment, instrumental task: F[4,65]=2.295, p=0.07; Pavlovian task: F[4,63]=1.526, p=0.205).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-tests) showing no significant effects.

claim: Glutamate receptor antagonism (CNQX-MK801) reduced the probability of port entry during the DS in the instrumental task.
source: Infusions of either a mixture of the glutamate receptor antagonists CNQX and MK801 or the relatively non-selective dopamine receptor antagonist flupenthixol had similar effects to VP inactivation with GABA agonists in both tasks. Glutamate or dopamine blockade reduced the probability of port entry during the cue (Sidak p<0.001 for both), though only the effect of glutamate blockade was selective to the DS (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B; DS Sidak, p<0.001; NS Sidak, p=n .s.) whereas flupenthixol reduced the probability of port entry during both cue types (DS Sidak, p<0.001; NS Sidak, p<0.003).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (post-hoc tests) and reference to figures.

claim: Dopamine receptor antagonism (flupenthixol) reduced the probability of port entry during both the DS and NS in the instrumental task.
source: Infusions of either a mixture of the glutamate receptor antagonists CNQX and MK801 or the relatively non-selective dopamine receptor antagonist flupenthixol had similar effects to VP inactivation with GABA agonists in both tasks. Glutamate or dopamine blockade reduced the probability of port entry during the cue (Sidak p<0.001 for both), though only the effect of glutamate blockade was selective to the DS (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B; DS Sidak, p<0.001; NS Sidak, p=n .s.) whereas flupenthixol reduced the probability of port entry during both cue types (DS Sidak, p<0.001; NS Sidak, p<0.003).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (post-hoc tests) and reference to figures.

claim: Glutamate or dopamine antagonism selectively increased port entry latency during the DS but not during the NS in the instrumental task.
source: Glutamate or dopamine antagonism selectively increased port entry latency during the DS (CNQX-MK801 Sidak, p=0.005; flupenthixol Sidak, p=0.022), but not during the NS.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (post-hoc tests).

claim: Glutamate or dopamine antagonism significantly reduced port entry probability during the CS+ but not during the CS– in the Pavlovian task.
source: In the Pavlovian task, glutamate or dopamine antagonism, like inactivation, significantly reduced port entry probability during the CS+ (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B; CNQX-MK801 Sidak, p<0.001; flupenthixol Sidak, p=0.043), but not during the CS–, and had no effect on port entry latency (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (post-hoc tests) and reference to figures.

claim: Glutamate or dopamine antagonism had no effect on port entry latency in the Pavlovian task.
source: In the Pavlovian task, glutamate or dopamine antagonism, like inactivation, significantly reduced port entry probability during the CS+ (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B; CNQX-MK801 Sidak, p<0.001; flupenthixol Sidak, p=0.043), but not during the CS–, and had no effect on port entry latency (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to figures.

claim: Infusions of the NK-1 antagonist WIN51708 had no effect on port entry probability or latency in either task.
source: Infusions of the NK-1 antagonist WIN51708, used to block the effects of substance P, had no effect on port entry probability or latency in either task.
evidence: The claim is supported by the absence of significant effects in the statistical analysis.

claim: VP neurons do not drive movement invigoration generically, but encode a variable that is manifested by port entry latency after instrumental, but not after Pavlovian training.
source: Our results demonstrate that VP neurons do not drive movement invigoration generically, but encode a variable that is manifested by port entry latency after instrumental, but not after Pavlovian training.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference from the differential encoding and functional effects observed across tasks.

claim: Manipulations of VP alter a wide range of motor behaviors including general locomotion.
source: Manipulations of VP alter a wide range of motor behaviors including general locomotion (Churchill and Kalivas, 1999; Kitamura et al., 2001; Napier and Chrobak, 1992; Root et al., 2015), though reports of locomotor activation linked to VP may be more related to activity in nearby structures such as the rostral preoptic area (Zahm et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies on VP and locomotion.

claim: Reports of locomotor activation linked to VP may be more related to activity in nearby structures such as the rostral preoptic area.
source: Manipulations of VP alter a wide range of motor behaviors including general locomotion (Churchill and Kalivas, 1999; Kitamura et al., 2001; Napier and Chrobak, 1992; Root et al., 2015), though reports of locomotor activation linked to VP may be more related to activity in nearby structures such as the rostral preoptic area (Zahm et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation suggesting alternative anatomical explanations.

claim: VP neuron activity may contribute to at least some forms of flexible approach, but only when that approach reflects a specific underlying decision variable.
source: VP neuron activity may contribute to at least some forms of flexible approach, but only when that approach reflects a specific underlying decision variable.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference from the observed task-specific encoding patterns.

claim: VP activity has been suggested to signal many different decision-making variables including action values or state values.
source: VP activity has been suggested to signal many different decision-making variables including action values or state values (Ito and Doya, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: One critical difference between cue responses in the instrumental versus Pavlovian tasks may be the degree to which state values are linked to action values.
source: One critical difference between cue responses in the instrumental versus Pavlovian tasks may be the degree to which state values are linked to action values (Averbeck and Costa, 2017).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to relevant theoretical work.

claim: VP neuron activity may represent the incentive value of both the instrumental DS and the Pavlovian CS+, but the latency to approach the reward location following Pavlovian cues does not reflect this incentive value.
source: Within this framework, VP neuron activity may represent the incentive value of both the instrumental DS and the Pavlovian CS+, but the latency to approach the reward location following Pavlovian cues does not reflect this incentive value (Ahrens et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2015; Robinson and Flagel, 2009).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Proximity encoding is similar in the two tasks, but is only correlated with latency encoding in the instrumental task.
source: This is supported by our finding that proximity encoding is similar in the two tasks, but is only correlated with latency encoding in the instrumental task.
evidence: The claim is supported by the statistical analysis showing task-dependent correlation between proximity and latency encoding.

claim: VP activity both encodes and contributes to the likelihood of behavioral responses following the Pavlovian cue, though this encoding is weaker than in the instrumental task.
source: We should note that VP activity both encodes and contributes to the likelihood of behavioral responses following the Pavlovian cue, though this encoding is weaker than in the instrumental task.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings on response likelihood encoding and functional effects.

claim: VP activity may contribute to response likelihood in the Pavlovian task via the same underlying circuits and processes as in the instrumental task, or through distinct neural and psychological mechanisms.
source: VP activity may contribute to response likelihood in the Pavlovian task via the same underlying circuits and processes as in the instrumental task, or through distinct neural and psychological mechanisms, such as thencoding of incentive value versus expected reward value (Chan et al., 2016; Tindell et al., 2009), as some evidence suggests that reward value and motivation rely on dissociable neural mechanisms even within VP (Creed et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Rostral and caudal VP neurons have different morphologic and electrophysiologic properties.
source: Because rostral and caudal VP neurons have different morphologic and electrophysiologic properties (Bengtson and Osborne, 2000; Kupchik and Kalivas, 2013), and differentially modulate reward-related behaviors (Chang et al., 2017; Ho and Berridge, 2014; Johnson et al., 1993; Mahler et al., 2014; McBride et al., 1999; Panagis et al., 1995; Smith and Berridge, 2005), we previously assessed neural responses in the DS task in rostral, middle and caudal subregions of VP (Richard et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical and physiological studies.

claim: Rostral and caudal VP neurons differentially modulate reward-related behaviors.
source: Because rostral and caudal VP neurons have different morphologic and electrophysiologic properties (Bengtson and Osborne, 2000; Kupchik and Kalivas, 2013), and differentially modulate reward-related behaviors (Chang et al., 2017; Ho and Berridge, 2014; Johnson et al., 1993; Mahler et al., 2014; McBride et al., 1999; Panagis et al., 1995; Smith and Berridge, 2005), we previously assessed neural responses in the DS task in rostral, middle and caudal subregions of VP (Richard et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Most neurons in rostral, middle and caudal VP subregions exhibited excitations following the DS, and post-cue firing in 18–25% of neurons predicted response latency.
source: We observed similar population encoding at rostral, middle and caudal recording sites in VP, in that most neurons in each subregion exhibited excitations following the DS, and post-cue firing in 18–25% of neurons predicted response latency.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the authors' prior study.

claim: Neurons throughout VP appear to encode cue value and the subsequent reward seeking similarly across the rostrocaudal axis.
source: Although neurons throughout VP appear to encode cue value and the subsequent reward seeking similarly across the rostrocaudal axis, discrete populations may be differentially involved in dissociable behavioral responses to these reward cues (Milton and Everitt, 2010), including their ability to act as conditioned reinforcers (Mahler et al., 2014; Torregrossa and Kalivas, 2008) or to generate instrumental reward-seeking or other reward-related motivational states (Leung and Balleine, 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similar encoding patterns observed across VP subregions, with citations supporting functional heterogeneity.

claim: VP has previously been conceptualized primarily as a major output structure of the nucleus accumbens.
source: VP has previously been conceptualized primarily as a major output structure of the nucleus accumbens, which has been demonstrated to encode the value of reward-predictive cues (Ambroggi et al., 2008, 2011; Day et al., 2006) as well as both proximity to the response operandum and the vigor of subsequent reward-seeking actions (McGinty et al., 2013; Nicola et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and citations to prior literature on VP-accumbens connectivity.

claim: The nucleus accumbens encodes the value of reward-predictive cues.
source: VP has previously been conceptualized primarily as a major output structure of the nucleus accumbens, which has been demonstrated to encode the value of reward-predictive cues (Ambroggi et al., 2008, 2011; Day et al., 2006) as well as both proximity to the response operandum and the vigor of subsequent reward-seeking actions (McGinty et al., 2013; Nicola et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies on nucleus accumbens encoding.

claim: The nucleus accumbens encodes both proximity to the response operandum and the vigor of subsequent reward-seeking actions.
source: VP has previously been conceptualized primarily as a major output structure of the nucleus accumbens, which has been demonstrated to encode the value of reward-predictive cues (Ambroggi et al., 2008, 2011; Day et al., 2006) as well as both proximity to the response operandum and the vigor of subsequent reward-seeking actions (McGinty et al., 2013; Nicola et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies on nucleus accumbens encoding.

claim: The timing of nucleus accumbens and VP cue responses is inconsistent with the idea that VP cue responses are a reflection of upstream activity changes in the accumbens.
source: We previously showed that the timing of nucleus accumbens and VP cue responses is inconsistent with the idea that VP cue responses are a reflection of upstream activity changes in the accumbens (Richard et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work on timing analysis.

claim: Chemogenetic 'disconnection' of VP and accumbens during Pavlovian conditioning results in elevated sign-tracking behavior.
source: In addition, chemogenetic 'disconnection' of VP and accumbens during Pavlovian conditioning results in elevated sign-tracking behavior, suggesting a competitive interaction between these two sites (Chang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior study using chemogenetic methods.

claim: Post-cue excitations in VP neurons occur well before accumbens inhibitions.
source: Since nucleus accumbens inputs to VP are primarily GABAergic, the likeliest mechanism by which accumbens activity changes could result in VP excitations is via disinhibition: yet we showed previously that post-cue excitations in VP neurons occur well before accumbens inhibitions.
evidence: The claim is supported by a reference to the authors' prior timing analysis.

claim: Blocking the actions of substance P has no effect on the likelihood or latency of cue-elicited reward seeking.
source: Further, we show here that blocking the actions of substance P, the main known source of excitatory drive from the accumbens to the VP (Napier et al., 1995), has no effect on the likelihood or latency of cue-elicited reward seeking.
evidence: The claim is supported by the pharmacological manipulation data showing no effect of NK-1 antagonism.

claim: Local disruption of either glutamate or dopamine signaling was effective in reducing the likelihood and speed of cue-elicited reward seeking.
source: By contrast, local disruption of either glutamate or dopamine signaling was effective in reducing the likelihood and speed of cue-elicited reward seeking, indicating a role for both neurotransmitter systems in VP contributions to the invigoration of reward seeking.
evidence: The claim is supported by the pharmacological manipulation data showing effects of glutamate and dopamine antagonism.

claim: Both glutamate and dopamine signaling play a role in VP contributions to the invigoration of reward seeking.
source: By contrast, local disruption of either glutamate or dopamine signaling was effective in reducing the likelihood and speed of cue-elicited reward seeking, indicating a role for both neurotransmitter systems in VP contributions to the invigoration of reward seeking.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pharmacological effects observed.

claim: VP integrates glutamatergic inputs from a variety of brain areas implicated in reward learning and cue-elicited motivation.
source: VP neurons integrate glutamatergic inputs from a variety of brain areas implicated in reward learning and cue-elicited motivation (Fuller et al., 1987; Grove, 1988; Kelley et al., 1982; Maslowski-Cobuzzi and Napier, 1994; Reep and Winans, 1982; Záborszky et al., 1984), including the medial pre-frontal cortex (mPFC) (Capriles et al., 2003; Ishikawa et al., 2008a, 2008b; Moorman and Aston-Jones, 2015; Peters et al., 2009; Stefanik et al., 2013) and the basolateral amygdala (BLA) (Ambroggi et al., 2008; Ishikawa et al., 2008b; Jones et al., 2010a, 2010b; McDonald, 1991; Perry and McNally, 2013; Záborszky et al., 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to anatomical and functional studies.

claim: Excitatory drive from the BLA onto VP neurons has been shown to be modulated by local dopamine following stimulation of the VTA.
source: Excitatory drive from the BLA onto VP neurons has been shown to be modulated by local dopamine following stimulation of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Maslowski-Cobuzzi and Napier, 1994; Napier and Potter, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: Inactivation of the VTA reduces the likelihood and increases the latency of instrumental responding.
source: Importantly, inactivation of the VTA reduces the likelihood and increases the latency of instrumental responding (Fischbach-Weiss et al., 2018), including DS-elicited reward seeking (Yun et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies on VTA inactivation effects.

claim: VP neurons selectively encode and contribute to the vigor of cue-elicited reward-seeking actions when those actions are trained via an instrumental contingency, rather than via Pavlovian conditioning.
source: Here we demonstrate that VP neurons selectively encode and contribute to the vigor of cue-elicited reward-seeking actions when those actions are trained via an instrumental contingency, rather than via Pavlovian conditioning.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings from the electrophysiology and pharmacology experiments.

claim: VP encoding of vigor is not related to motor invigoration or reward expectancy per se, but to the ability of reward-related cues to invigorate actions upon which reward is contingent.
source: These results indicate that VP encoding of vigor is not related to motor invigoration or reward expectancy per se, but to the ability of reward-related cues to invigorate actions upon which reward is contingent.
evidence: The claim is a summary interpretation of the findings showing task-specific encoding and functional effects.

claim: VP cue responses do not merely reflect motor invigoration, but encode a motivation signal that may be integrated in the VP.
source: Together, our results show that VP cue responses do not merely reflect motor invigoration, but encode a motivation signal that may be integrated in the VP.
evidence: The claim is a summary interpretation of the findings, suggesting VP's role in motivation rather than simple motor control.
